subtopic: MARRIAGE OF CANADIANS BY CONSULAR AGENTS ABROAD
MARRIAGE OF CANADIANS BY CONSULAR AGENTS ABROAD
speechtext:
1.	Are Canadian diplomatic or consular agents empowered to marry Canadian citizens abroad?
2.	Can Canadian citizens be married abroad by diplomatic or consular agents of the United Kingdom and, if so, under what statutory provision or agreement can this occur?
3.	Since the Statute of Westminster of 1931, has the government of Canada requested the government of the United Kingdom to continue to allow its agents to marry Canadian citizens outside Canada?
4.	Does the government of Canada intend to allow this practice to continue?

subtopic: MARRIAGE OF CANADIANS BY CONSULAR AGENTS ABROAD
speechtext:
1. The Canadian diplomatic or consular agents do not have the power to solemnize abroad the marriage of Canadian citizens.
2.	Canadian citizens are able to marry abroad in accordance with the provisions of local law. As an additional facility, by virtue of the United Kingdom Foreign Marriage Act of 1892-1947 and the Foreign Marriages Order 1964, which empowered certain official British representatives abroad to perform marriages abroad, Canadian citizens can, if they wish it and provided they meet the requirements involved, be married abroad by such officials.
3.	Canada has not made such request to the Government of the United Kingdom.
4.	The British legislation in this field has been useful to those Canadians desiring to take advantage of it. The question as to whether this procedure should be maintained is, however, under study.
Legislative authority in relation to marriage is divided between the provinces and parliament. The provinces have jurisdiction in relation to "solemnization of marriage in the province" and parliament has jurisdiction in relation to "marriage and divorce". As a consequence, while parliament could authorize Canadian consuls abroad to perform marriages, it would be necessary for the provinces also to pass legislation validating such marriages.
Federal legislation would be required since such marriages would not relate to a solemnization of marriages in the provinces and therefore would not be within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. Jurisdiction on this question would be vested in the parliament of Canada. However, provincial legislation would also be required so as to ensure that marriages solemnized outside the provinces would be valid within the provinces. Only the legislature of the province could enact a law declaring that a marriage solemnized outside the province is a valid marriage within the province. It will be realized that the concurrence of the province would therefore be required in order to change the actual practice. The question is presently under study.

subtopic: MAILING OF SAVINGS BOND INCOME TAX FORM
MAILING OF SAVINGS BOND INCOME TAX FORM
speechtext:
1.	When Canada savings bonds interest payments
were sent out on November 1, why was a notice Included stating that the T5 form would be mailed not later than February 28,	1968, rather than
including this form with the interest payment as has been done previously?
2.	What is the estimated cost of making this second mailing to all registered bond holders?
Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAILING OF SAVINGS BOND INCOME TAX FORM
speechtext:
1. Because holders of fully registered Canada savings bonds who redeem their bonds up to August 31 in each year receive accrued interest to date of redemption from the bank branch which redeems them, the records at Ottawa must be adjusted to allow for these transactions before any cheques can be prepared. By the time all such bonds reach Ottawa from bank branches coast to coast and have been processed, the time remaining for cheque preparation is limited. The number of holders of fully registered Canada savings bonds is now so great that if the cheques and forms T5 were both to be prepared in time for all of them to reach bond holders by November 1st, expensive additional equipment, which would only be used for a short time each year, and more staff would have been required. Of total production time, about two thirds is needed on forms T5 and one third on cheques, whether they are produced in one operation or two.
2. By delaying production of forms T5 until after the cheques are prepared additional costs have been avoided which would be much larger than the stationery mailing and other costs involved in the present separate despatch of T5 forms.

subtopic: CANADIAN FOREIGN ASSETS NATIONALIZED
CANADIAN FOREIGN ASSETS NATIONALIZED
speechtext:
1. Has the government any record showing the number of claims Canadians have made in connection with their assets in other countries which have been nationalized without compensation and, if so, what are such claims and in what countries?

2.	Is the government of Canada negotiating with those countries so that the Canadians concerned will receive fair compensation?
3.	Has the Cuban government nationalization program affected Canadian industries or capital and, if so, has the government of Canada taken any steps to protect Canadian interests?

subtopic: CANADIAN FOREIGN ASSETS NATIONALIZED
speechtext:
1. Yes. Pursuant to understandings reached with the Governments of Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Czechoslovakia, the Department of External Affairs has requested and received from Canadian citizens details concerning property in these countries which has been nationalized, expropriated or otherwise taken without compensation. In addition, the Department has on record a number of nationalization claims which have arisen in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Yugoslavia, Cuba, the United Arab Republic and Communist China, as well as in the Eastern zone of Germany. These claims have resulted, generally speaking, from the nationalization or other taking of urban real property, residential property, farm land, industries, bank accounts and other debts, bonds, mortgages, etc. However, pursuant to a well-established principle of international law, the Canadian Government can advance only those claims which belonged to the Canadian citizens at the time of loss and continuously thereafter until the presentation of the claims to the foreign governments.
2. A settlement of Canadian claims against Bulgaria in respect of nationalized property was reached on June 30, 1966. Under an Anglo-Yugoslav agreement signed on December 23, 1948, a former owner of expropriated property in Yugoslavia, who had Canadian citizenship or other British subject status at the time and who gave due notice of claim, could have obtained limited compensation. Canadian officials have held to date three rounds of negotiations with Hungarian authorities in an attempt to reach a lump-sum settlement of Canadian claims against Hungary. A fourth round will begin on November 27. Negotiations toward a lump-sum settlement of claims against Poland are expected to begin early next year and it is hoped that it will be possible to start negotiations next year as well with Romania and Czechoslovakia. Consideration is being given to raising with certain other governments the claims of Canadian citizens in respect of property which has been nationalized or otherwise taken.
November 27, 1967

3.	Yes. The Canadian Government has succeeded in obtaining payment of certain commercial debts owing to Canadian companies. Other such commercial debts are currently under discussion with the Cuban authorities, as is the question of nationalizations.

speechtext: I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister about the public exchange of criticism between the Prime Minister of Canada and the president of France which took place earlier today. I think I may be permitted to say, quite apart from the merits or demerits of what was said on either side, that this is an extraordinary way to carry on international relations.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO EXCHANGE BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext: My question is, could the Acting Prime Minister give the house any helpful information on the background and circumstances of this exchange, and in particular could he tell us whether the remarks of the Prime Minister preceded those of General de Gaulle, were contemporaneous, or were made subsequently, and was this exchange entirely accidental or was it in any way planned?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO EXCHANGE BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my belief is that the speech made by the Prime Minister this morning in London when he received the freedom of the city was completely unrelated to the remarks made by the president during the course of a press conference. As a matter of fact I have been advised that when the Prime Minister was about to take his plane he was advised that observations had been made by the president of the French Republic. The Prime Minister's reply was that he would not make any comment until he had seen the text. My own examination of the Prime Minister's speech bears out the view that the two statements were completely unrelated.
While I am on my feet, I should like to answer another part of the question and this I shall do in French.

We have just received the first reports of the press conference given by the president of France. However, there seems to be certain doubts about his exact statement about Quebec.
Of course, before deciding, the government will have to consider carefully the statement of the president of the French Republic. But I can add even now that the government, in considering these texts, will keep in mind two main considerations: On the one hand, our

traditional and steadfast friendship for France and, on the other hand, our obligation, as a government representing the whole country on the international level, to exercise our rights and to allow no interference in our domestic affairs.

speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Could the Acting Prime Minister obtain for the house an official text of the remarks made by our Prime Minister in London at the Mansion House luncheon, and could the Acting Prime Minister use the offices of the Department of External Affairs to obtain an official transcript from France of what the president of France said there so the two texts could then be made available to the house?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on November 17 last I put a question to the Minister of Transport which could be summarized as follows: Can the minister confirm whether there will be winter navigation on the Saguenay river? If so, will his department provide icebreaker service to keep the channel open on the river this winter?

subtopic: SAGUENAY RIVIER-INQUIRY AS TO WINTER NAVIGATION
speechtext: What we did last year, as I understand it, was to make some probes into the river to determine the feasibility of maintaining navigation. The proposal is to repeat the process this year in order to gain additional information. It would be the intention of the department to attempt these probes at a time when the operation might be most beneficial to the ships which would like to use these waters during the winter months. There seems to be insufficient traffic at the moment to require that continuous icebreaking facilities be made available. Mr. Chairman, the agreement which we have made will make it simpler for me to deal with this matter now. I do not intend to address any of my remarks to the amendments moved by members of the New Democratic party. I will wait until they are dealt with by the Registrar General. With respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yukon, I think the arguments in its favour have been well put. I will simply summarize them and leave the matter there in view of the length of time which has already been taken in dealing with this measure.
It is the view of this party that this bill is innocuous, that there is no need for it to be brought forward, that all the powers which are purported to be given to the minister and

But in order to try to make something out of the bill, an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Yukon. It provides that the minister will have the right not only to engage in research but also in investigation.
Particular reference is made to price increases. It is our view that the primary interest of the consumers lies in the increases in prices which have taken place all across the country. We doubt very much that the federal government has sufficient authority in this regard, and we have made this plain during the course of speeches we have already made. It is our view that the government laboured mightily to produce a misshapen, distorted and twisted mouse with its head where the tail should be and its tail where the head should be. The hon. member for Essex West attempted to reform that distortion by an amendment which put consumer affairs at the head and corporate affairs at the tail. However, this did not have more appeal to us so far as the bill is concerned. We are simply asking that the minister pursue the right of investigation in order to try to determine to what extent the federal government may be able to help the sorely pressed consumer at the present time.
We have made particular reference to price increases in our amendment and in the concluding part have suggested that the minister should report to parliament with his recommendations with regard to this matter. We feel that the government is insinuating through this measure that it may be able to work its way into fields in which it has no jurisdiction.
The problem of fraud has been mentioned. Every sale of an article is a question of civil rights. Every province has legislation dealing with the sale of goods and every province has statutes dealing with fraud. Unless these frauds amount to criminal acts they lie exclusively in the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Restrictive trade practices lie exclusively within the jurisdiction of the federal government. Consumer credit is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and advertising, unless it is of a misleading nature, can be the subject of criminal proceedings. Unless the government is prepared to declare that certain acts are criminal in their nature and will provide penalties for them, it has no jurisdiction in that field.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
Under this amendment we propose that the government examine this issue to see to what extent it can, within the framework of the legislation and of clause 6 of the bill, discover whether there is any possibility in conjunction with the provinces of dealing with the very serious problem of price increases. We recognize that the problem of price increases lies within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance and not within that of the Registrar General. As a result of a motion made not so long ago by the Leader of the Opposition we are forbidden to comment on the bad management of the government which has brought about price increases. It was obvious by the vote which was taken at the time that the majority of the supporters of the government, including the Registrar General, accept the fact that the government has managed the finances of this country in a most efficient, economic and careful way and that if price increases have taken place it is someone else's fault and not that of the government.
This being the case, I cannot touch on that matter, but I can say that with the spiral of inflationary price increases which is going on, both because of the government's actions as well as in spite of them, people may take advantage of the situation to establish wage and price increases which are not consistent with the requirements of the time. This may be an area where the government, after suitable investigation in the closest co-operation with the provincial governments, might delegate to some board sufficient responsibility to deal with this issue in cases where there have been glaring and flagrant abuses leading to an inflationary spiral of costs of goods, services and wages.
We move this amendment with that in mind. If the government really intends to do something, then I suggest that the minister can well lend his support to the amendment, and I ask members of the committee to support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have looked at this amendment with the care which its author indicated it deserves. I want to say at the outset that we reject completely the initial remarks of the hon. member for Peace River which were of course merely an echo of those made by his colleague, the hon. member for Yukon, when he presented the case of the official opposition at the second reading stage, namely, that the department will have no teeth.
I said in closing the debate on second reading-and with your consent, sir, I think I


should answer the argument advanced again today-that this bill does not set forth the entire consumer program of the government. It does not elaborate or describe the powers which will be made available to the department to enforce a consumer program. It empowers the minister and the department to protect consumer interests. It empowers the minister and the department to initiate new measures having to do with consumer interests. The teeth are already in legislation on the statute books of Canada, and this legislation spans the authority of several government departments. The purpose of this bill is to co-ordinate government policy which affects the consumer, to render this legislation more enforceable, to ensure that enforcement is applied on a more uniform basis and to ensure that the legislation is observed and enforced from the point of view of the consumer, a (3:40 p.m.)
There is a good deal of legislation already on the books, Mr. Chairman. I mention section 306 of the Criminal Code relating to misleading advertising, section 33 (c) of the Combines Investigation Act involving the same subject, and the food and drug regulations. There are the series of measures relating to the misleading description of agricultural and fisheries products and legislation under the Canada Corporations Act relating to the disclosure to the public of information in the hands of financial institutions. This and other legislation which we would propose as the department assumes its authority will constitute the teeth in favour of the consumer in so far as this bill is concerned.
This bill gives the department the muscle to exercise and to clamp down with those teeth. So any argument suggesting that the bill does not contain teeth flows from a misreading of the nature of the bill and what it is attempting to do, namely, to co-ordinate and enforce on a uniform basis the existing legislation on the books and give it a perspective, an orientation which is, primarily, the protection of the Canadian consumer.
Turning to the wording of the amendment itself, I may say that what the amendment purports to do is add the power of investigation to clause 6, subclause (2) concerning the power of research. I suggest that what the amendment purports to do, if accepted by this committee, is completely illusory. The minister already has the power of investigation under the provisions of clause 5 of the bill relating to combines and bankruptcy. These powers of investigation are found
November 27, 1967	COMMONS
within the Bankruptcy Act and the Combines Investigation Act. The difficulty here is that this clause would attempt to add new powers of investigation without in any way indicating how these powers would be co-ordinated with the powers that already exist.
I want to say as well that the great difficulty with this amendment is that it purports to give the power of investigation without in reality conferring any power to investigate because any power to investigate should provide the terms of reference and the consequences of such an investigation. Where is the power to compel witnesses? Where is the power to limit the nature and extent of the investigation or inquiry? Where are the limits placed upon the invasion of private rights? In every statute setting forth specific powers of investigation, the limits of the investigation are carefully set forth. Thus, in section 3(a) of the Bankruptcy Act the powers are indicated in clear terms relating to the conduct, dealings and transactions of the bankrupt concerned, the causes of the bankruptcy and the disposition of the property. The powers of inquiry are specifically set forth in that section. There are no powers contemplated in this amendment to implement the investigation.
In the Combines Investigation Act section 8 gives the director of research and investigation power of inquiry but the limits of that inquiry are carefully set forth in part V of that statute as the subject matter of the investigation-offences in relation to trade, conspiracy, mergers and monopolies, price fixing, resale price maintenance, refusal to sell or supply goods. In other words, the terms of reference protect the subject from undue encroachment by anyone launching an inquiry. I want to suggest to the committee in the strongest terms that this amendment is toothless because while it sets forth an assumed power of investigation, in fact it confers no power upon the minister at all, no power to compel witnesses, no power to compel attendance, no power to compel the production of documents. On the other side, and even more important, it does not set limits on the terms of reference which would protect the individual from undue encroachment by an inquiry.
I want to say that when we were discussing this bill amongst ourselves we discussed whether or not it should have a power of inquiry. One of the difficult aspects was how to limit that power of inquiry in strict terms of reference, how to define the subject matter over which the inquiry would be conducted

Corporate and Consumer Affairs without invading severely the rights of people and institutions to resist an inquiry that might be an unwarranted encroachment upon those rights by one minister granted this power within a statute. I want to say that the power of inquiry already exists in the government under the Inquiries Act, and should matters arise of sufficient importance in the opinion of the government to cause such an inquiry to be launched, then the government would do that. However, one must be very careful, I submit to the committee, how one confers the power of inquiry upon a single minister, and it should be done only under a provision which carefully restricts and defines the terms of reference.
Another point of disturbance was the constitutional limitation of such an inquiry power. The hon. member for Peace River quite properly outlined to the committee some areas that lie within provincial jurisdiction and some areas that are shared between the federal and provincial authorities. The consumer interest is shared by both federal and provincial authorities. The purpose of this bill is to confer upon one minister the authority to co-ordinate federal policy relating: to consumer interests with those authorities: having the same jurisdiction within provincial governments. I want to say that an unlimited power of investigation might well provoke constitutional problems. If a minister were unilaterally to embark upon an inquiry which transgressed upon the constitutional field of the provinces, and this amendment makes no reference to limiting the scope of an inquiry, this might well involve challenges in the courts.
In rejecting this amendment, therefore, I want to say that we have not yet fully explored the scope of the existing legislation or its administration and if it should happen, after we become more aware of the responsibilities conferred upon this department, that a specific inquiry power should be lodged in one minister, at that time we would come back to parliament to ask for it. However, we would ask for it in terms that would give the minister power to investigate, power to compel attendance, power to produce documents, power to swear witnesses, and even more important from a civil rights point of view, with definite limits to the scope of the power of inquiry.
Our primary objection, then, to this amendment is that it tends to give the department or the minister the illusion of having an investigatory power, because it uses the word "investigation", without the

Presumably the minister thinks that the existing legislation which deals with these problems of consumer affairs is adequate.
Speaking from my experience in this house over the past 16 years, it seems to me that one of the great difficulties in protecting the consumer arises because the legislation designed to deal with combines, mergers, monopolies and restraint of trade, lacks teeth. I remember that one of the first debates in which I participated in this house had to do with the abolition of resale price maintenance. That was in the fall of 1951. The measure was put forward by the Liberal government of the day. It was thought that the measure would resolve all consumer problems with respect to constantly rising prices. Actually the legislation has been instrumental in eliminating more and more

confirmed something that we have been claiming which has been borne out by recent events. The only real purpose of establishing this department is to give the minister, as I have said before, a forum in which he may promote his candidacy for the leadership of the Liberal party.
During the last week we have seen what has been going on in this country. Noranda Mines increased its copper prices. We have been lectured by ministers of the crown such as the Minister of Finance, by editorial writers of large newspapers, by financial analysts in our daily newspapers and by others about the danger of inflation and about the danger of pricing ourselves out of the world market. We have been told to use restraint. I am disturbed that most of these lectures seem to be directed at one group in our country, the ordinary citizens, the ordinary workers. Essentially, the workers are being told: For goodness sake, make sure that your union does not demand too much because the economy cannot afford it. Such exhortations would have a good deal more force if those making them would say something when business increases its prices and profits, particularly when there is no justification for price increases.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
On November 21, six days ago, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported that Noranda Mines proposed to increase the price of copper from 47 cents to 51 cents a pound. From that day to this, questions have been asked in this house almost daily in an attempt to find out what the government proposes to do. We received the ingenuous answer a few days ago that Noranda was being very generous in raising its price by only 10 per cent and not to 60 cents a pound. I suppose we could say "Thank God for small mercies".
Why has this increase been decided upon? There is a simple answer. There is at the present time, and there has been for some five months, a strike directly affecting all the copper mines in the United States, and as a result of the tremendous demand for copper brought about by prosperity in the United States and the war in Viet Nam there is an acute shortage of that metal. There is a demand for copper almost regardless of price. So Noranda and other producers such as Hudson Bay Mining and International Nickel can charge any price they wish.

What are the effects of this increase likely to be? In the issue of the Globe and Mail to which I have already referred, that of November 21, the reactions of some of the users of copper are reported. We find Mr. James Thomas, vice president of Phillips Cables of Brockville, saying that the increase is "definitely inflationary." He is reported as commenting:
The increase and subsequent additions will mean a 20 to 30 per cent increase in the cost of wire and cable.
He went on to say that an addition in the cost of primary metals would obviously be felt in the prices of finished goods. Mr. E. W. Darby, secretary of Pioneer Electric which manufactures transformers and switchgear apparatus, said he was shocked by the news. The increase would force the company into an increasing use of aluminum.
Copper is used in almost every manufacturing and industrial process in this country. One thinks immediately of power generators and the lines which carry power, of refrigerators and other appliances. It is hard to mention an item in which copper is not used. One might think that this price increase was forced upon the company, and upon others which will undoubtedly follow suit, by falling profits or higher costs. But the figures which appear in the Financial Post surveys do not indicate this to be the case. We find that Noranda Mines made a profit of around $31 million in 1964. In 1965 it had risen to $36 million and in 1966 to $43 million, an increase of almost 50 per cent in three years.
Here are similar figures with respect to the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company. In 1963 net profits amounted to $11 million. Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly to this amendment, first in respect to its substance and, second, on the ground of admissibility. On second reading we engaged in a debate involving a prices review board. I outlined to the house then, and would ask the indulgence of the committee to underline now, the fact that the movement of prices is due to many complex factors, many of which are beyond the control of the federal government and many of which are beyond the jurisdiction of any of the governments of Canada. A good many of them, of course, are related to international economic factors, particularly in our vulnerable economy which depends, as it does, on foreign trade for one-quarter of every dollar earned. The movement of prices depends, within the private sector, on wage settlements, on rising costs in other areas and on the production process. In so far as it relates to government spending it depends in large measure not only on spending at the federal level but also on spending at the provincial and municipal levels.

In 1966, for instance, the federal government spent $6.7 billion on goods and services and at the same time the provincial and municipal governments spent $12.6 billion. Two thirds of every tax dollar spent by governments in Canada on goods and services was spent at the provincial and municipal levels. Despite the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway as to the constitutional limitations upon our ability to control prices, those limitations do exist. In times other than those of emergency or of war the responsibility for the control of prices and wages rests with provincial authority. As I said before, at the federal level we can influence prices in the sense of ensuring that competitive forces are at play. The department has the responsibility for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act, the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act and other legislation which can inject competition, particularly at the manufacturers' level.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
If the purpose of the prices review board is to control prices, which is often indicated by members of the New Democratic party at the hustings level although they would have us believe in the house that its purpose is only to review prices, it would be constitutionally invalid. Such a prices review board would be toothless. As drafted the amendment purports to require the minister to set up a board with the authority to inquire. But the minister cannot give any board real powers of investigation because those powers would have to be spelled out in the Act. But there are no powers in the amendment to compel the attendance of witnesses, to compel the production of documents, to compel testimony to be given. So here again, as I said with respect to the amendment presented by the hon. member for Yukon, the amendment is illusory in this respect.
The proposed amendment envisages board authority to make inquiries but it sets no limits on such inquiries; in other words, it does not set out within its terms what the limits are upon the infringement of civil rights by any such board. It does not set out the limits of any inquiry. It does not tell us just what protection would be given to the average citizen in this country with respect to the powers of inquiry or the invasion of civil rights contemplated here.
The amendment speaks of joint action with the provinces, but joint action of an undetermined kind. What kind of joint action is envisaged? What is meant by the words
November 27, 1967	COMMONS
"deal with price increases"? Are the provinces to be asked to pass complementary-legislation? I remember that when dealing with this matter on second reading the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the leader of his party, suggested that a prices review board would have to be supplemented by complementary, simultaneous legislation passed by all the provincial governments.
The hon. member thereby admitted that there was a constitutional limitation upon this type of board and that the authority over price control lay with the provinces. Would such a prices review board have a role to play with respect to the major determinants of prices, namely, wages and other incomes? If not, these inquiries would be meaningless. Unless the proposed board is to be purely advisory, it is doubtful that parliament is competent to legislate in this field, and if it is purely advisory the amendment is unnecessary because clause 7 of the bill provides authority to establish advisory boards.
I am not yet convinced that a prices review board would be a practical measure. Do the advantages of such a board outweigh the costs, both monetary and social? Do the actual money costs of setting up such a board, together with the social costs of the delay and the red tape, really justify it?
I wonder whether hon. members of the New Democratic party have thoroughly thought out some of the consequences that might flow from the establishment of such a board. It might cause the setting of artificial prices based on a substantial rise in cost. It might allow any manufacturer to justify a price increase if he could substantiate an increase in cost, without having at the same time to show that he had done everything possible to improve his product, to improve the distribution process, to improve unit productivity, research, and so on.
Since an increase in cost will be primarily,
I suppose, a result of an increase in the cost of labour, it might be that a union, knowing a wage increase would justify a price increase before such a prices review board and knowing that this increase in cost would be passed on to the consumer whether or not it was justified by productivity, would be tempted to press for that wage increase. As Professor Beach of McGill University said in a recent speech in Montreal to the Consumer Association of Quebec, there is in a prices review

Corporate and Consumer Affairs board "a strong built-in tendency to inflation." I want to quote some of his words:
It may come as a shock to some here when I say that a cost increase is not an adequate justification for a price increase. If costs increase and squeeze profits the industrialist should attempt to improve his product or his process, and only as a last resort will prices be raised-the last resort which may well imply losses and bankruptcy for some.
The inability to pass on cost increases is a great social control-even uncertainties about the abilities to pass on such costs is important. Thus I am not in favour of a price review board. It has more dangers than promises of success.
It is the opinion of Professor Beach that it has inherent in it as many dangers as it has promises for success. I have grave doubts as to the admissibility of this amendment, Mr. Chairman.

The first ground is that the amendment is moved to a money bill, which has been preceded by a resolution necessary for the introduction of a money bill, and that the amendment would tend to add to the expenditure of money within the precedents recognized by the house. I refer Your Honour first

of all to citation 246, paragraph 3, page 207 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, which reads as follows:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the Crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the Crown has demanded or recommended a charge. And this standard is binding not only on private members but also on ministers whose only advantage is that, as advisors of the Crown, they can present new or supplementary estimates or secure the royal recommendation to new or supplementary resolutions.
I submit to you, sir, as chairman of the committee that in attempting to add a subclause establishing a prices review board the amendment goes not only beyond the scope of the resolution which preceded the introduction of the bill but also extends the scope, object and purposes of the bill by adding the creation of a new board.
I want to refer Your Honour also to citation 249 (1) found on page 214 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, which reads as follows:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian Commons receiving the authority of the Crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer. On one occasion, in the English Commons, the consent of the Crown was given to certain formal resolutions proposed by a private member with reference to charges in courts of law to be defrayed out of the consolidated fund. It was thought, however, that any resolution placing a charge on the consolidated fund should be moved by a minister of the Crown, and the more regular procedure was thereupon carried out. It was distinctly affirmed, however, that the member who proposed the motion involving the charge was within his right when he had the sanction of the Crown, but it was generally admitted at the same time that it was better, as a matter of policy, that the proposition should emanate from a responsible adviser of the sovereign.
The responsibility of recommending applications for pecuniary redress or relief to the consideration of parliament should rest solely upon the executive government, who are strictly accountable for every item of public expenditure, whose especial duty it is, in the interest of the taxpayers, to oppose all unnecessary outlay, and who possess peculiar facilities for investigating into the merits of all pecuniary claims.

The hon. gentleman has already indicated he has no intention of controlling prices. So the bill as it stands is just another shade of pale so far as the consumers are concerned.
The minister has in the course of the past few years built up a picture of himself as an affable, nice fellow, a friend of everyone including the corporations. If he is to discharge his present job effectively as minister of corporate and consumer affairs I do not think it is possible for him to maintain this image in the community, especially among the creme de la creme of the corporate elite. He needs to buy himself a barbed wire overcoat and thump these people around a little. If he is not willing to do this, the bill becomes just one more piece of window dressing such as have been perpetrated on our people for the last 100 years.
Every time the question of prices comes up someone blames increases in wages right away. No one asks why it is that wages have increased. Look at the levels of corporation profits. It is these profits and their effect upon prices which have caused labour to rectify the situation by bringing back some of this money into their own pockets. What

Corporate and Consumer Affairs the minister seems to have envisaged in connection with this bill is the appointment of a little debating society, a couple of ladies discussing the price of shoelaces while doing their knitting. What is going on in this country is not even unbridled free enterprise because, as my hon. friend from York South has told us, we are really living today under a system of monopoly. There was no reason for the recent increase in steel prices with extra profits for the steel companies. Yet no justification was ever offered in defence of that action.
Almost every phase of this nation's industrial activities is controlled by two or three large corporations, mostly foreign owned, which do not care two hoots about the Canadian consumer and are entirely unconcerned about his welfare. Does anybody believe that General Motors could not run Ford and Chrysler off the market any time they saw fit? The only reason Ford and Chrysler are allowed in Canada is to maintain this patchwork system of so-called free enterprise. General Motors know that if they run Chrysler and Ford off the market the United States government would intervene. This is why they continue this pretence of competition which is not competition at all.

subtopic: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF SUPPLEMENT INTO BASIC PENSION-PAYMENT AS OF RIGHT AT AGE 65

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF SUPPLEMENT INTO BASIC PENSION-PAYMENT AS OF RIGHT AT AGE 65
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Old Age Security Act to provide for the full amount of the income supplement provided thereunder to be incorporated into the basic pension, and for the eligible age to be lowered immediately to 65, so that all persons in Canada 65 years of age or over who meet the residence requirements will receive the full pension of $105 per month without any income test, the full amount of the old age security pension thus being recognized as a matter of right.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the terms of the resolution which Your Honour has just read from the chair are quite clear. It is our view

November 27. 1987

that the full amount of the old age security-pension, which is $105 a month at the present time, should be paid to all our old age security pensioners without any income or means test on any portion of it. It is also our view that the provision for the old age security pension to be payable at age 65 should come into effect immediately, rather than on a year to year basis as is the case at the present time.
Obviously, the presenting of this resolution is an expression of opposition to the idea of an income or means test on any portion of the old age pension. In case anyone has forgotten it-and I find that hard to believe-we in this party took a very strong stand against the so-called income test which was put on the extra $30 that was added to the old age security pension by legislation enacted in 1966. We felt then that it was wrong in principle to take this retrograde step. We still feel it is wrong in principle and that parliament should call upon the government to take action to correct the mistake that was made in 1966.
When I think of the debates we had on this matter last year, I am aware of the fact that arguments were put forward both ways. I am also aware of the fact that it was felt in some quarters that we should try this method for a while to see how it would work out. But I suggest that the experience of our people has already demonstrated it was a retrograde step that the government asked parliament to take.
I have been actively interested in old age pensioners and old age pension legislation long enough now to have seen three phases of it so far as our people are concerned. I saw for a good many years the effects of the original old age pension act, with its means test, on our older people. I am talking about the pension that was initially $20 a month, which rose by stages to $40 a month, was payable only at age 70 and had a means test on it. I remember very well how in those days the people who drew that pension felt the stigma that went with it. They were not happy to say they were on the old age pension because it meant they had submitted to a means test and were in dire circumstances.
Then I lived through the period, as most of us in this house have, when we had an old age security pension the full amount of which was free of a means test of any kind. That was true from January, 1952, until the end of 1966. During that time it became a matter of pride for older people to be able to say they were on the old age pension. In the
Old Age Security
earlier years of that 14-year period the amount was a little more valuable to people than has been the case more recently, but even apart from the amount there was a definite change in the attitude of people toward the old age pension, both those who received it and those who did not, because it was completely a matter of right.
Now we are in a third period, the period of a means or income test on a portion of the pension. It has been in effect for only ten or 11 months and yet already my mail and my contacts tell of hundreds of people who are feeling the indignity of the income test to which they have to submit. I regret as strongly as I can the fact that parliament took this retrograde step. I also regret the fact that there seems to be a tendency to say in this place: Oh, we have dealt with the old age pension question. Why don't you leave it alone for a while?
To support the statement I have just made that there are people who are unhappy about the way in which the income or means test is affecting them, may I cite one particular kind of grievance to which, as a matter of fact, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) alluded in a question he put to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) on the orders of the day this afternoon. I remind you, sir, that when we were debating the so-called guaranteed income supplement the theme, the insistence of the minister was that under this legislation people would be brought up to a minimum figure; no old age pensioner would have any less than a total of $105 a month. One of the guarantees the minister gave when we were debating this legislation was that if a person's income changed during the course of a year from what he had estimated it would now be, an adjustment could be made. This is not true for all our pensioners.
I have cases-and I have spoken to the hon. member for Ontario since he asked his question today and find he has precisely the same kind of cases in his experience-where this principle that the minister guaranteed is not being carried out. Let me boil it down to one instance. I will call this woman Mrs. M., because her story has been written up by a columnist in the Winnipeg Tribune. Mrs. M. is a woman who at the time her husband died in 1962 was awarded, by the company for which he had worked, a five-year pension. I am not commenting on the fairness or rightness of such a pension, but it is a fact that she was awarded a five-year pension which ran from the spring of 1962 until the

of age and who may be able to retire by accepting a slightly smaller pension than he could get if he continued to work until the age of 65. He has asked for my advice and I told him that amongst other things he should consider the future of our economy. 1 asked him whether he thought he could get by for the rest of his life on the pension which he will receive now at the age of 60. I said to him, "Look, my friend, you are in good health and you are only 60 years old. You have a good chance to live to the year 2000. Do you think that the pension you are now able to draw will be good enough for the conditions of life in the year 2000?" The answer is, no; some arrangement must be made for pensions to escalate.
I produce this argument with regard to retired civil servants at least once a week, but I think this will have to be done for all our people, and it is logical and sensible to accept the proposition that the over-all old age security pension without a means test must go up progressively as the years go by. It is not sufficient to grant a supplement on the basis of a means test. Ever since I put this resolution on the order paper on May 9 asking that the full pension of $105 a month be paid to everyone without a means or income test of any kind, conditions have changed to such an extent that now I would have to amend the figure of $105 a month to $125 a month because of the way in which costs have gone up since then and the way in which the living standard has gone up. I say to hon. members that there is no point in being shocked at the idea of this further increase. The standard of living of other people is going up. We think that people who retire, whether it is at the age of 60 or at the age of 65, should not be asked to live for the rest of their days on the same amount of money and thereby have to take a gradual decline in their actual as well as their relative standard of living.
Therefore, as I said, if I were proposing this resolution today I would go a step further and say that the old age security pension should be $125 a month rather than $105. But one cannot change the resolution at this point, and I would emphasize my contention that the most important part of this motion is not the amount of money that is mentioned in it but rather the principle of universality. Let me repeat again-and I know I have said it in the house hundreds of times-that one of the finest things we ever did was back in the early 1950's when we adopted a universal old age pension. All our
Old Age Security
people received it as a matter of right. Parliament took a retrograde step when we put part of it on an income test, and I hope we will soon get back to the progressive position we took in the early 1950's and pay the full old age security pension to all as a matter of right.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to deal with the motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I should like to place on record the position of our party regarding the period which has just elapsed. We believe that the means test incorporated in the legislation put forward by the government some months ago was the meanest test of all, particularly when inflation and high costs are a part of the everyday life of our communities and particularly in view of the fact that this measure affects those people who have contributed so much in the past to the productive capacity of our nation today. I agree with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that assistance should be made available to our senior citizens at the age of 65 without the escalating feature which was incorporated into the legislation brought forward by the government some time ago.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I know there are those who will say that the government cannot find the money to provide this assistance. If that argument is valid, then it is valid when applied to other expenditures the government has been making. We should compare them on a priority basis to ascertain whether or not this argument holds water. I think of the expenditures being made on behalf of the C.B.C. amounting to $140 million and perhaps next year $180 million. I think of the plight of the senior citizens of our country and I cannot help but feel that part of the money expended on the C.B.C. probably could have gone to help these people had proper priorities been established by this parliament and by the government. I think of the expenditures that were made by Canada in order to have Expo. I am one of those who believe that the expenditures made for Expo were well spent. Here again, however, we find that a tremendous amount of money has been spent in order that we might celebrate the centennial of our confederation.
When we have asked questions of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) with regard to the possibility of a centennial bonus of $100 for our senior citizens, we have been met by silence. I

November 27, 1967
Old Age Security
say to you, sir, that this ill becomes a government that is trying to celebrate the centennial of our confederation.
In talking about our senior citizens at this time I want to add one additional argument to indicate what could have been done. I remind you, sir, and members of the house that since this government came into office some four years ago more than 10,000 civil servants have been added to the payroll. This represents 300 members of the civil service for each member of the government elected in 1963. In other words, the cost that Canadians have had to bear in order to have a Liberal government during the past four years has been an additional 300 civil servants for each member of the House of Commons elected by the Liberals in 1963. If we say that these civil servants are on a modest salary of something like $5,000 or $6,000 each and each has a secretary being paid about $4,000 with office equipment at $1,000 or $2,000 each, we have an expenditure per civil servant of $10,000. If the true figure were known, it would probably be twice that. The minimum cost, therefore, of these civil servants would have been about $3 million. This cost is being borne entirely by the people of Canada in order to sustain this government in office, and yet the government says it cannot grant the senior citizens of this country the things that are set out in the resolution we have before us.
When we have asked for a centennial bonus for the senior citizens of this country, government ministers have been silent. When a resolution like this is before the house we find the Minister of National Health and Welfare absent, not caring enough to be here to listen to the debate and let us know why the government has not seen fit to make this provision.
I say to you, sir, that had the government wished to take care of the senior citizens of this country, had they established proper priorities, we could have provided this assistance without in any way endangering the orderly development of our nation. After all, when we look at the swollen civil service we have today, when we realize some of the waste that is taking place in departments that have been built up in the way the Department of Industry has been, then I cannot help but ask those on the government benches to give a little more consideration in working out priorities and try to do something to meet the challenge embodied in this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to speak tonight on this most important motion.
I have often listened most attentively and respectfully to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He is an experienced parliamentarian who never misses an opportunity to make a valuable contribution to the debate in this house.
Nevertheless, when I heard him speak on social security, more particularly on the old age pensioners and guaranteed income supplement to the aged starting at 65 years of age, I realized how much easier it is to sit on the opposition benches than on the government side.
I am, however, most happy to rise in this debate, because I am a member of the party that fathered almost all, if not all, the social security measures benefiting Canadians today from ocean to ocean.
Mr. Speaker, in spite of these objective remarks, I must say that 1 share the feelings of the mover of this motion to the effect that we should aim more and more at a wider distribution of social security, thus giving greater justice to all but, obviously, when a question of social justice is involved, social equality must be more particularly mentioned, not social inequality.
If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, in order to make my meaning clearer, I shall review certain facts and quote statistics which will enable us to better grasp the situation.
As a matter of fact, the Canadian parliament has already recognized the need to maintain incomes by passing, in 1966, an act on the guaranteed income supplement. The purpose of that plan is to ensure old age security pensioners a monthly minimum income of $105, during 1967, by adding a supplement of up to $30 a month to the pension of those who have no other source of income. The plan also provides, for 1968 and subsequent years, the possibility of increasing the guaranteed minimum income, according to the increase in the cost of living.
Indeed, those increases have been announced and they will become effective in 1968, for both the old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement.
At the most, those increases will boost the payments to $107.10 per month. I am convinced that the income supplement plan now in force gives our old people an income more efficiently and at a lower cost than would be
November 27, 1967



the case under a formula such as the one proposed by my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
In fact, we do not need that formula, because the income supplement plan meets the needs of the present situation better.
One of the great advantages of the guaranteed income supplement is that it allows for calculating the payments granted in terms of an estimated income.
The motion of the hon. member would make this supplement universal and would provide an additional income to many people who do not need it.
In September 1967, a total of 1,244,085 senior citizens were covered by the Old Age Security plan; of this number, 717,845 pensioners, or 57.7 per cent, received partial or full payment of the guaranteed income supplement. These figures mean that, in 1967, there were 526,960 pensioners, or 42.3 per cent, eligible to Old Age Security allowances, whose income exceeded the permissible limit for payment of a guaranteed income supplement, namely, $1,620.
Of those who received guaranteed income supplement allowances, 436,011 pensioners, or 60.7 per cent, were entitled to full payment, while 281,834 others, or 39.3 per cent, were entitled to partial payment.
The motion introduced by my hon. friend would increase these payments for all pensioners. This would not only increase expenditures, but it would also be unfair toward pensioners with moderate or relatively high incomes.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would result in a considerable increase of costs. The expenditures thus added to relate the total amount of the supplement to all pensioners receiving old age security payments in 1968-69 would reach about $300 million. Additional expenses caused by the decision to extend these payments to all those between 65 and 66 years of age in 1968-69 would be about $200 million; accordingly, the amount of new expenditures for 1968-69 caused by this proposal would run to about $500 million. This would bring about an increase in expenditures for 1968-69 totalling about $2 billion.
Of course, when considering these things -objectives are always praiseworthy-we must understand that, as administrators, we are delegated to attend to proper management of the country's business and to pass adequate legislation.
Old Age Security
I often hear members on the other side of the house, and especially from the hon. member's party, saying that the government does not do enough. If we were to carry into effect all measures and good suggestions submitted to us, we would fall into such excesses that the government would be the first to show the way to inflation by increasing its public expenditures.
However, every time mention is made of increasing taxes or imposing new measures requiring the co-operation of all citizens, then the government is accused of taking dollars from the taxpayer's pockets. Such a situation is normal. The hon. member who has been here for a long time has certainly made his mark, since he has always kept the confidence of his constituents, but we must say that, at the present time, in 1967, we distribute, we administer the funds committed to us, but we cannot work miracles. That does not exist in the public service.
We must administer without a deficit and in a climate of social justice. We must not throw off balance the small wage-earners, those who want to benefit from that social equality, for instance.
The problems of the old, which I feel very deeply, must be considered quite objectively but they must be solved with equality in mind.
For instance, I know very well that if I were 65, today or tomorrow, and arrived in my constituency, I would not need a guaranteed income supplement, but I would be happy if the majority of my constituents, who are not as well off, who worked hard for their children, who did not spare their health or their time, and who contributed also to the old age security fund as citizens, received a supplement. All that would help promote social justice and the welfare of the population.
The additional amounts suggested in that motion would in most cases go to people who tend to be great consumers, and that would increase the demand for consumer goods and services. As a result, other increases would have inflationary effects on prices and costs. The additional expenses should be supported out of the old age security fund. On the other hand, various taxes would have to be increased: personal income tax, corporation-

Social justice surely demands that we consider the mass and those excellent suggestions in the future. But let us use them today to eliminate the present situation and to give us a truly complete social mechanism.
I feel that, at the present time, it is urgent that Canadians should be given a decent health insurance program. I am pleased that the present minister is dynamic, extremely perspicacious, and that he has the social security of all Canadians at heart, just like his predecessors in the past.
The newspaper La Patrie of Montreal published an eloquent article on poverty on June 4, 1967. It is often said that the poor and the old are ill more often, that they need medical assistance oftener. I think that with the savings of the wise administration we now have, we will be able to give Canada and the Canadians a health insurance that will give greater social equality and allow, once again, the central government to assert itself and say to the provinces: We have something to present, we have something to give you; you are free to refuse it or to accept it, but the government of Canada wishes to bring, from sea to sea, social justice to all Canadians, English-speaking, French-speaking, or whatever the language they may speak.
I think that when we relieve someone of hardship, hunger, when we create social equality, when we pass legislation as did this government, when we pass a bill which is complete, that is unpartitioned, but which

takes into account social facts, then we are doing something for Canada, we are doing something for its people, because when one is happy, when one has a homeland, one of course has something to live for, to hope for, a striking example to pass on to future generations. In fact, I think that the most striking example is to be able to say that, in this house, we have contributed to the improvement of social security, we have contributed to establishing not perfection of course-since perfection is unknown in this world and no one is naturally perfect-but something concrete. In my opinion, we have all the qualities, the sense of liberalism required to see things as they must be seen, all across Canada, and with a very broad outlook.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
We must be proud enough to tell those people: We would like everybody to get $105 per month at 65 or even at 60 years of age,, but the economic situation does not allow for such a provision.
I know some 50 or 55 year old unemployed who come to my office. They are pitiful. I would like to help them. I think that these citizens, who are understanding people, will realize that this is for the future good of the whole people; they can be proud to be Canadians, because not only their fellow-Canadians, their parents and their friends, but above all their children, will be able to take part in progress and in a better Canadi-anism. I am convinced that it is good administration on the part of the government which allows us to reach that goal.
This is my first term in this house, and I fully appreciate the extraordinary work done by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the members of the cabinet, the ministerial team and the right-thinking people in this house. I am proud, at this time in our history, to belong to a government which stands up, assumes its responsibilities and protects, with much concern for equality- because equality is always relative-the true democratic rights of all the citizens of all nationalities.

Mr. Chairman, any monetary or financial system that does not take into account the question of prices is bound to fail. Sooner or later, it must face the phenomena of inflation and deflation. What use then the monetary units we have in our pockets if the prices of products offered to consumers increase in the same proportion?
Now, in what way does the Social Credit technique for price adjustment limit the freedom of producers and distributors in setting their own sale price? Does the government bureaucrats know the cost price of goods offered for sale better than the producer?
The producer alone must set the conditions which he feels are most appropriate to the production process to meet the needs of the Canadian consumers, but it is not for him to set or determine the conditions under which the consumers will get his products; that is to say, the producer cannot be denied his right to get paid in full according to his sale price, but it does not matter to him if the money he receives comes in full from the consumer or if part of that money has been issued by a credit organization whose creation we recommend.
Such price adjustment could also be made at set periods, every six months or once a year. It can be called a general discount applied to all retail products. That discount could be repaid to the retailer through the issuance of credit.
This bookkeeping operation would enable buyers to pay only a set fraction of the price of the item wanted and the merchant would be compensated for the difference through a credit opened by the authorized office.

The committee found that Canadian drug prices were among the highest in the world, up 140 per cent in the past 16 years compared with 40.8 per cent for general consumer goods, and returning profits double that enjoyed by other manufacturing industries.
As an indication of what is happening to the consumer, I should like to quote from the minutes of the special committee on drug costs and prices for Thursday, December 1, at page 1512. The hon. member for Winnipeg North is questioning the witness about government policy on buying drugs and the prices paid by the government as compared with prices paid by consumers. The record reads:
Mr. Chairman, just for the record, I would like to point out that the department was able to purchase at the price of $3.25 per one hundred, and that Parke Davis, which is the big manufacturer or distributor in Canada, offered them to the department for $6.39 per one hundred.
I made a phone call after we got this table. The list price which Parke Davis offers to retail druggists in Canada is $39.40 a hundred; the discount which the druggist gets is 40 per cent. The
November 27. 1967

retail druggist therefore pays $23.64 for one hundred of these capsules which Parke Davis offered to the department for $6.39 a hundred. I think it is an interesting comparison.
-on Librium, I notice that here again prices were asked for 10 milligram tablets in bottle sizes of 100 tablets. I notice that Hoffmann-La Roche, which tendered the lowest price offered them to the department for $2.60 a hundred in bottles of 100 tablets. The price to retail drugstores by Hoffmann-La Roche is $12 a hundred, list price.
There are many examples of this type that could be placed on the record. It is generally acknowledged by those who have looked into the situation that the drug industry is in deplorable shape and needs some corrective action. If this department of consumer affairs is to serve a really useful purpose, then it must take action to bring down the prices of drugs. We do not believe that the bill, as it is now constituted, possesses the power to use effectively all the instruments that the minister might be able to use on behalf of the consumer. The willingness of the government to consider our proposal will be an indication of how serious it is in tackling this problem.
I should like to read into the record an article written by Mr. D. H. Fullerton which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen for November 25. The writer raises these very interesting questions:
Action to bring down Canadian drug prices continues to move at a snail's pace.
In June the sales tax on drugs was removed, although most observers felt that this step should have awaited measures to bring greater price competition into the business.
Current proposals being considered by the government involve compulsory import licences and changes in the Trade Marks Act, which would increase the effectiveness of import competition.
Unfortunately, even if these proposals become law there is some doubt whether the impact on drug prices will be more than marginal.
In a society where the high cost of drugs is borne by those least able to afford it-the old, the sick and the poor-one may be pardoned for asking why action on drugs has not had a higher priority.
One answer is being observed in Ottawa today where the well-heeled, monopolistic, and internationally powerful drug industry has been recently mounting the most intensive lobby ever seen in the capital.
A senator with impeccable political connections is acting as contact man for the industry. Ministers, senior officials-irj fact anyone who is likely to have any possible role in drug policy-are being wined and dined and courted by the manufacturers.
Several new plants are being promised for certain key constituencies-as if new jobs for a few hundred workers would counterbalance the $200 million or more the country is paying annually in excessive prices for drugs!
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
The effectiveness of the drug lobby was plainly demonstrated at hearings of the commons committee on drug costs and prices. One M.P. was openly being fed information and questions by representatives of the companies and of their organization, the P.M.A.C., in order that he could better interrogate witnesses hostile to the drug manufacturers.
The minister has an opportunity tonight to indicate that some of these charges are not true. He can take positive action to curtail the influence and power of the drug companies in Canada. I suggest that influence and power is being used against the consumer.
As an indication of the kind of reprehensible approach the drug companies take, I have a letter sent to me by a doctor who resented the infantile approach of these drug companies to the members of his profession. The letter has at the top a picture of two little capsules. I will not read it into the record because it is too lengthy. However, the letter, in child-like terms, goes on gently to lead the doctor to consider that these two capsules might not be alike, but it does not give him any adequate reason for saying so.
This letter is from Bristol Laboratories of Canada Limited, and is put out by a firm that at the moment is under investigation in the United States for price fixing. I should like to quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of October 24, 1967 which reads:
After six years of delay, the drug industry's battle of the century has begun in Federal District Court here.
The adversaries are the justice department and three of the nation's largest drug manufacturers- Chas. Pfizer and Co. Inc., American Cyanamid Co. and Bristol-Myers Co. These are charged in a three count indictment with fixing artificially high prices and monopolizing the manufacture, distribution and sale of the "wonder" antibiotic drugs that millions of Americans use.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister that even tariff removal on drugs, or complete free trade between Canada and the United States would not be effective in solving the problem of consumers in Canada of procuring drugs at the prices they should be paying. The same companies that are operating in the United States are operating in this country, and if they are fixing prices, arranging prices or whatever they may be doing in the United States, I think it is reasonably certain the same thing will be happening in this country. All that the removal of the tariff will accomplish will be to allow the companies to rationalize a little better than they have in the past.
The impact on drug users would be minimal. Far more than that has to be done in
November 27, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs order to bring this industry to heel. We believe that a provision should be included in this bill to permit the government to establish a crown corporation which could manufacture drugs, or could buy them from Canadian companies and put the government brand on them. These drugs could then be distributed directly to druggists. The crown company could operate with a minimum of advertising and could generally serve to rationalize the industry on behalf of the consumer.
What we are suggesting is not original. The government does this now on behalf of many of its own agencies. If I may, I should like to quote again from the minutes for December 1 of the special committee on drug costs and prices for December 1, page 1500. Mr. I. C. Ellis, pharmacist for the Department of National Health and Welfare is being questioned about suppliers, and he said:
-the Department of National Health and Welfare does have a variety of programs. We all seem to go along in different directions in the procurement of drugs. The medical services branch, which covers the activities of the Indian health services and northern health services, sick mariners services and civil service health, requires pharmaceuticals and continuing supplies in varying amounts.
9 (8:50 p.m.)
The Emergency Health Services Division of the Health Services Branch require large annual purchases of drugs and pharmaceuticals for additions to, and resupply of, the national stockpile.
There is also a general purchasing branch in the Department of Defence Production charged with the responsibility of procuring a very wide range of commodities, and among these commodities are drugs.
The amounts are not insignificant. As reported at page 1526 of the same report, in reply to a question about the amounts, Mr. Erskine stated:
Mr. Chairman, in total dollar value I could not tell you. Certainly it is a very small percentage of individual types of drugs; but we have not yet any statistics for the two departments that are fairly new customers of ours. We have some estimates of their total requirements in a year. I think around 31 million is what we expect. The Department of National Defence would run anywhere from $750,000 to $1 million, and National Health and Welfare would be relatively small, perhaps $100,000.
So you can see, Mr. Chairman, about $5 million worth of purchases are accounted for by Mr. Erskine. What we are suggesting is that this program, which is now operated in a somewhat divided way, be grouped together and then extended so that purchases in

bulk be made not only on behalf of government departments but also on behalf of the consumers of this country. I do not anticipate that this corporation would take a very large proportion of the business in drugs in this country; but if the government were to move into this field and indicate that it intended to take action to bring down the price of drugs by this method, then the industry would soon straighten itself out very quickly. If they did not do so, the government would take over some of their business.
There has been experience of this situation in other countries. For example, in Sweden the co-ops undertook the job. They effectively reduced prices in many areas, just by moving into the market and taking a small portion of business in the market. The other companies in the field got the message very quickly and reduced their prices to a more reasonable level.
The minister has previously pointed out in argument the difficulty of establishing what is a fair price, or how one arrives at a price. I would suggest that one of the ways to establish this is in a competitive market. However in order to be sure that the price is as competitive or as low as it could possibly be under the circumstances, there must be real competition. This we have not had in the drug industry in this country. Therefore I suggest that the minister has an obligation on behalf of Canadian consumers to see that such competition and alternate supply exists for the consumers, and is obligated to seek powers in the bill that enable him to do so.
Hospitals all across Canada are now doing exactly what I am suggesting the minister should do. They are buying drugs on behalf of the consumers, who ultimately pay the hospital bills. I would therefore suggest that the minister give very careful consideration to this proposal and indicate his willingness and concern to take real action on behalf of the consumers by accepting the amendment I should like to move at this time. My amendment is as follows:
That sub-clause (1) of clause 6 be amended by adding thereto, immediately after paragraph (d) thereof, the following new paragraph:
"(e) establish a corporation on behalf of Her Majesty which shall be empowered to: manufacture, sell, distribute, and promote drugs offered for sale in Canada;
supervise all advertising and promotion activities related to drugs including the distribution of samples and the content of advertising literature."

draw attention to proposals which could make it a far better piece of legislation if they were adopted. The bill in its present form is deceiving the people of this country, and unless it is improved we shall be the first to point out its shortcomings.
